latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Anatomic obstruction of the biliary tree (most often choledocholithiasis, also benign/malignant stricture, occluded stent, parasitic plug, hepatolithiasis) producing a closed, high-pressure space proximal to the block. This is the upstream necessary condition for cholangitis and the lever that source control must release.

Ascending colonization of stagnant bile from the duodenum (or via portal/hematogenous seeding through a colonized stent), with rapid growth of enteric gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter), enterococcus, and anaerobes in patients with biliary-enteric communication. Activity scales with stasis duration and bile pressure.

When intrabiliary pressure exceeds ~20 cmH2O, infected bile is forced across hepatocyte tight junctions and around bile canaliculi into hepatic sinusoids and perihepatic lymphatics, translocating bacteria and endotoxin into the systemic circulation. This is the mechanistic step that converts a local cholestatic infection into bacteremia/sepsis.
Bloodstream invasion by translocated biliary organisms; positive blood cultures occur in roughly 20-50% of cases and dominate by Enterobacterales. Drives systemic inflammatory and septic responses.

Endotoxin and PAMP exposure activate TLR4/NF-kB and inflammasome pathways with surge of IL-6, TNF, IL-1, and acute-phase reactants. Drives fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin rise, and rigors.

Back-pressure cholestasis plus inflammatory injury to cholangiocytes and periportal hepatocytes. Produces a predominantly cholestatic enzyme pattern (ALP/GGT and direct bilirubin elevations greater than ALT/AST), with secondary modest hepatocyte injury.

Distributive vasodilation, microcirculatory failure, and hypoperfusion produce hypotension, AKI, hepatocyte stress beyond cholestasis, encephalopathy, and DIC physiology. Severity defines Tokyo Guidelines Grade III and is the dominant near-term mortality driver.

Persistent or partially treated cholangitis can seed periportal liver parenchyma with abscess formation, especially with delayed drainage, intrahepatic stones, or partial-segment obstruction. Detected as hypoattenuating hepatic lesions on CT/MRI; requires drainage in addition to antibiotics.

Septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system as a complication of severe or delayed cholangitis/hepatic abscess. Produces persistent bacteremia, abdominal pain, and may seed liver further. Requires anticoagulation consideration plus prolonged antibiotics.

Successful ERCP/PTBD/surgical drainage releases the closed-space pressure, halting cholangiovenous reflux and allowing antibiotics to reach the focus. Latent variable that captures the treatment-context state of source control adequacy.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bile stasis behind an obstruction permits enteric organisms ascending via the sphincter of Oddi (or seeded from a stent) to multiply unchecked; flow normally clears bile.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: M_AC_BILIARY_OBSTRUCTION must be active to maintain pressure
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacterial replication plus continued bile production in an obstructed system raises intraductal pressure above the cholangiovenous reflux threshold (~20 cmH2O), forcing infected bile across hepatocyte junctions into sinusoids and lymphatics.
Independent pressure contribution from obstruction itself; severity of obstruction modulates reflux threshold crossing.
Reflux is the direct conduit for biliary organisms into hepatic veins and the systemic circulation, producing positive blood cultures.
LPS from gram-negative organisms triggers TLR4/NF-kB signaling and acute-phase cytokine release.
Sustained cytokine activation produces vasoplegia, endothelial dysfunction, microcirculatory failure, and the hypoperfusion phenotype of septic shock.
Bile retention itself injures cholangiocytes and periportal hepatocytes through bile acid toxicity and back-pressure.
Direct cholangitic inflammation amplifies cholestatic enzyme release beyond pure obstruction.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk amplified by delayed/incomplete drainage, intrahepatic stones, or segmental obstruction
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sustained cholangitic inflammation can extend periportally and form pyogenic abscess foci, especially with retained intrahepatic stones.
Periportal suppuration extends into adjacent portal venules producing septic thrombophlebitis.
Septic clot in the portal venous system can continuously shed organisms, increasing bloodstream bacterial load and making bacteremia persist despite partial source control.
IL-1/IL-6/TNF act on hypothalamic set-point producing the high spiking fevers and rigors typical of cholangitis.
Bacteremic surges in cholangitis classically present with shaking chills/rigors.
Cytokine and fever-driven sympathetic activation raises heart rate; further increased by hypovolemia/shock.
Cytokine-driven respiratory drive plus metabolic acidosis compensation raises respiratory rate.
Acute-phase response mobilizes neutrophils with marked leukocytosis; severe sepsis may instead produce leukopenia.
Neutrophilic predominance with band forms (left shift) is typical.
Bone marrow release of immature neutrophils signals bacterial sepsis.
IL-6 drives hepatic CRP production; CRP often >100 mg/L in cholangitis with characteristic 24-48 h lag.
Procalcitonin rises sharply with bacteremia and tracks closely with severity in cholangitis.
Obstructive cholestasis raises total bilirubin, predominantly direct (conjugated).
Conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into sinusoids when canalicular flow is blocked.
Cholangiocyte induction of ALP (and GGT) by bile acids produces the canonical cholestatic enzyme pattern.
Periportal hepatocyte stress produces moderate ALT/AST elevation, usually less marked than ALP/bilirubin; transient very high transaminase spikes can occur with stone passage.
Co-elevation with ALT in cholestatic injury; AST often higher than ALT in older patients.
Clinically visible jaundice (the J of Charcot's triad) appears once total bilirubin exceeds ~2-3 mg/dL.
Distention of the biliary tree produces visceral RUQ/epigastric pain (the P of Charcot's triad), often colicky if from stone.
Distal CBD obstruction causes proximal duct dilation visible on US/CT/MRCP; threshold ~6-7 mm (more with prior cholecystectomy or age).
Intrahepatic ducts dilate when obstruction is sustained or proximal; activity scales with severity and chronicity.
Bile sampled at ERCP/PTBD is positive in the great majority of cholangitis cases; bile culture defines the local pathogen.
Bacteremia produces positive blood cultures in 20-50% of episodes; rate higher with severe disease.
Enterobacterales dominate the microbiology of cholangitis bacteremia.
Vasoplegic shock and capillary leak produce hypotension, the H of Reynolds' pentad.
Same hemodynamic axis as MAP; SBP is what is typically charted at the bedside.
Hypoperfusion and septic encephalopathy (the M of Reynolds' pentad) reflect Grade III severity.
Tissue hypoperfusion drives anaerobic metabolism; lactate >2 mmol/L marks tissue stress, >4 mmol/L predicts mortality.
Septic AKI from prerenal hypoperfusion and intrarenal microcirculatory injury.
Prerenal azotemia and impaired clearance during septic AKI.
Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) is an early KDIGO criterion in septic AKI.
Sepsis-associated thrombocytopenia from consumption, marrow suppression, and DIC physiology; thrombocytopenia is part of TG18 Grade III criteria.
Coagulation dysfunction from DIC physiology and reduced hepatic synthesis (compounded by vitamin K malabsorption from cholestasis); INR >1.5 is a TG18 Grade III criterion.
Cholestasis impairs intestinal vitamin K absorption, reducing factors II/VII/IX/X; correctable with parenteral vitamin K.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Only in DIC physiology; in early sepsis fibrinogen rises as acute-phase reactant
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Consumptive coagulopathy in advanced DIC drops fibrinogen below acute-phase elevation.
Microthrombosis and reactive fibrinolysis raise D-dimer in sepsis/DIC.
Lactic and renal acid retention lower serum bicarbonate.
Septic ARDS and capillary leak can cause hypoxemia; less common than hemodynamic failure but contributes to severity.
SOFA aggregates the multi-organ dysfunction signal that defines TG18 Grade III cholangitis.
Grade III is defined by organ dysfunction (cardiovascular, neurologic, respiratory, renal, hepatic, hematologic).
Imaging detects hypoattenuating hepatic lesions when abscess formation has occurred.
CT/MR venography reveals portal vein thrombus with surrounding inflammation.
Direct pathway to septic shock without timely drainage and antibiotics.
Septic AKI is a frequent organ failure in cholangitis.
Severe gram-negative sepsis from cholangitis is a classic DIC trigger.
Septic ARDS can complicate severe cholangitis.
Direct mapping from latent obstruction mechanism to the source-control state axis used by treatment logic.
Biliary obstruction defines the biliary source for source control planning.
Cholangitis is one of the few infections where source control (drainage) is essentially always required.
Stone extraction, stenting, or external drainage relieves the mechanical block.
Pressure release halts ongoing translocation, the mechanistic core of why drainage rapidly clears bacteremia.
Successful drainage is the operational definition of adequate source control here.
Untreated bacteremia in cholangitis has mortality approaching 100%; modern series with timely drainage and antibiotics report 2-10% (Grade I-II) and 10-30%+ (Grade III).
Multi-organ dysfunction is the strongest predictor of in-hospital mortality.
Failure or delay of biliary drainage beyond ~24-48 h in severe cholangitis sharply raises mortality.
Inadequate empiric coverage (e.g., ESBL, carbapenemase) is a major reversible mortality driver.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Cholestatic pattern co-elevation; both share the obstructive driver but ALP rises with characteristic lag.
Direct bilirubin is the dominant fraction in obstructive pattern.
Sustained obstruction dilates the CBD upstream; acute obstruction may not yet show full dilation.
Successful drainage by definition reduces obstruction state.
Defervescence within 24-48 h of effective drainage is a clinical hallmark; persistent fever beyond this signals failure.
Bilirubin falls progressively over days after successful drainage with cholestatic enzymes lagging further.
Active coverage reduces clinical nonresponse, but persistent obstruction can still produce nonresponse despite active drug.
Persistent clinical signs after 48-72 h on appropriate antibiotics is most often a source-control problem rather than a drug problem.
Grade III is operationally defined by organ dysfunction.
Mortality scales steeply with TG18 grade.
Free communication with bowel raises anaerobic and enterococcal recovery rates and mandates broader empiric coverage.
Indwelling stents bias colonization toward resistant gram-negatives over time.
Stent biofilms harbor Pseudomonas and other healthcare-associated organisms.
Segmental obstruction by intrahepatic stones is a classical setup for pyogenic abscess.
Inactive empiric coverage is among the strongest modifiable predictors of mortality in gram-negative bacteremia.
Delay to drainage and antibiotics increases sepsis severity and mortality.

Antipseudomonal activity is an advantage over ceftriaxone in healthcare-associated cases.
Requires renal dose adjustment; risk of acute kidney injury and seizures at high cumulative doses.
Anaphylaxis history precludes use.
Antibiotics alone insufficient; drainage essential.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reasonable empiric option for community-acquired Grade I cholangitis without ESBL/Pseudomonas risk; metronidazole added when biliary-enteric communication or severe disease is present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbapenem is the empiric standard for ESBL gram-negative bacteremia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric choice for Grade III cholangitis, healthcare-associated cases, prior ESBL colonization, or prior antibiotic failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rising community E. coli resistance to aminopenicillin/BLI makes this less reliable for moderate-severe cholangitis; reserved for Grade I in low-resistance settings.
Inactive against ESBL.

treatments.context_specific_role: Narrow-spectrum option for community-acquired Grade I cholangitis in regions with low aminopenicillin resistance; not appropriate when E. coli resistance >20%.

QTc prolongation, tendon rupture, dysglycemia, CNS effects.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Urgent ERCP within 24 h is the central intervention in Grade III; Grade II needs early ERCP within 24-48 h; Grade I within 24-72 h or once sepsis controlled.
Roux-en-Y or unreachable papilla pushes to PTBD or EUS-guided drainage.
Coagulopathy raises sphincterotomy bleeding risk; correct with vitamin K/FFP or use balloon sphincteroplasty/stent without sphincterotomy.
Thrombocytopenia <50 raises bleeding risk; transfuse before sphincterotomy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Used in expert centers when ERCP fails, especially with malignant distal obstruction.

supportive_care: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid; early lactate-guided hemodynamic optimization for severe disease
NPO with IV maintenance fluids until clinical improvement and procedural plan defined
Strict input/output monitoring; consider arterial line and urinary catheter in severe disease
Frequent reassessment of vital signs, mental status, and urine output for progression to Grade III
Serial lactate, CRP, bilirubin, ALP, creatinine, platelets, and INR to track response to drainage and antibiotics
Blood cultures (≥2 sets) before antibiotics; bile cultures at the time of drainage
Pain control with caution about masking peritonitis; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment
Antiemetics for nausea/vomiting
Glucose control in diabetic patients with sliding scale insulin during sepsis
Vitamin K replacement for cholestatic INR elevation, especially before sphincterotomy
Component blood product support (FFP, platelets, fibrinogen) for sepsis-associated coagulopathy or DIC as needed
Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients per ICU criteria
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with mechanical compression initially when coagulopathy present, then pharmacologic when feasible
Coordinated multidisciplinary management with gastroenterology/biliary endoscopy, interventional radiology, and surgery on call
Re-imaging at 48-72 h if clinical nonresponse to identify hepatic abscess, pylephlebitis, undrained segments, or alternative diagnoses
De-escalation of antibiotics to organism-targeted regimen once cultures and susceptibilities are available
Total antibiotic duration typically 4-7 days after adequate source control for uncomplicated cholangitis; longer for bacteremia, abscess, or pylephlebitis
Plan for definitive treatment of underlying etiology after recovery (cholecystectomy for gallstones, oncologic management for malignancy, dilation/stent revision for strictures)
Patient and family communication about diagnosis, severity grade, planned drainage, and complication risks; advance care planning if elderly/frail with high mortality risk
Discharge planning with outpatient follow-up imaging, stent exchange schedule, and surveillance for recurrence
